results.name: session_drift_late_minus_early
results.description: Yes-rate on trials in the last third of the session (trial_index >= 300) minus the first third (trial_index < 150); observed above the null means people drift toward "yes" over the session, a nonstationarity the stationary model cannot produce (below means drift toward "no").

results.name: digit_rule_near_nonmatch_yes_rate
results.description: In sets of 2+ examples sharing one final digit, yes-rate for non-example targets within 3 of some example whose final digit does NOT match; observed above the null means people still generalize by size to near neighbours despite the "ends in d" rule (the model's rule over-suppresses them), below means people reject them even more than the model.

results.name: size_principle_far_target_k_slope
results.description: Among "far" targets (>=15 from every example, final digit shared with no example, and coprime with every example), least-squares slope of yes-rate on number of examples k; observed more negative than the null means people tighten generalization with more examples (size principle) more than the averaged-similarity model does, more positive means less.
results.code:
# name: size_principle_far_target_k_slope
# description: Among "far" targets (>=15 from every example, final digit shared with no example, and coprime with every example), least-squares slope of yes-rate on number of examples k; observed more negative than the null means people tighten generalization with more examples (size principle) more than the averaged-similarity model does, more positive means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    ns = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    sets = ns.unique()
    exm = {s: np.array([int(v) for v in s.split(",")] + [-1000] * (4 - len(s.split(",")))) for s in sets}
    E = np.stack(ns.map(exm).values)[:, :4]
    k = (E > 0).sum(1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    valid = E > 0
    dist = np.where(valid, np.abs(E - t[:, None]), 1000)
    far = dist.min(1) >= 15
    digm = (valid & ((E % 10) == (t[:, None] % 10))).any(1)
    Ep = np.where(valid, E, 1)
    g = np.gcd(Ep, t[:, None])
    share = (valid & (g > 1)).any(1)
    sel = far & ~digm & ~share
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    if sel.sum() < 3 or np.unique(k[sel]).size < 2:
        return 0.0
    kk = k[sel].astype(float)
    yy = y[sel]
    return float(np.polyfit(kk, yy, 1)[0])

results.name: within_set_target_spread
results.description: Mean over number sets (with 3+ distinct targets) of the standard deviation across targets of the per-(set,target) yes-rate; observed above the null means people's generalization is more all-or-none across targets (sharper, rule-like gradients) than the model predicts, below means people are flatter/more uniform than the model.
results.code:
# name: within_set_target_spread
# description: Mean over number sets (with 3+ distinct targets) of the standard deviation across targets of the per-(set,target) yes-rate; observed above the null means people's generalization is more all-or-none across targets (sharper, rule-like gradients) than the model predicts, below means people are flatter/more uniform than the model.
def test_statistic(df):
    d = df[["number_set", "target"]].copy()
    d["y"] = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    cell = d.groupby(["number_set", "target"])["y"].mean().reset_index()
    g = cell.groupby("number_set")["y"]
    sd = g.std(ddof=0)
    n = g.size()
    sd = sd[n >= 3]
    if len(sd) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(sd.mean())

results.name: digit_rule_contrast_k_growth
results.description: For sets sharing one final digit, (yes-rate matching-digit minus non-matching-digit non-example targets) at k>=3 examples minus the same contrast at k=2; observed above the null means the "ends in d" rule strengthens with more examples faster than the model's (k-1)*log10 scaling, below means people already apply it fully at k=2 (the model under-applies it for pairs / over-scales with k).
results.code:
# name: digit_rule_contrast_k_growth
# description: For sets sharing one final digit, (yes-rate matching-digit minus non-matching-digit non-example targets) at k>=3 examples minus the same contrast at k=2; observed above the null means the "ends in d" rule strengthens with more examples faster than the model's (k-1)*log10 scaling, below means people already apply it fully at k=2 (the model under-applies it for pairs / over-scales with k).
def test_statistic(df):
    ns = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    sets = ns.unique()
    dig, kk = {}, {}
    for s in sets:
        ex = [int(v) for v in s.split(",")]
        ds = set(v % 10 for v in ex)
        dig[s] = (ex[0] % 10) if (len(ex) >= 2 and len(ds) == 1) else -1
        kk[s] = len(ex)
    d = ns.map(dig).values.astype(int)
    k = ns.map(kk).values.astype(int)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    padded = ("," + ns + ",")
    tstr = df["target"].astype(int).astype(str)
    ident = np.array([("," + a + ",") in b for a, b in zip(tstr.values, padded.values)])
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    def contrast(mask):
        a = mask & (t % 10 == d)
        b = mask & (t % 10 != d)
        if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
            return 0.0
        return y[a].mean() - y[b].mean()
    base = (d >= 0) & ~ident
    return float(contrast(base & (k >= 3)) - contrast(base & (k == 2)))

results.name: prime_set_prime_target_contrast
results.description: In sets of 2+ examples that are all primes, yes-rate for non-example prime targets minus non-example composite targets of the same parity as the examples' majority; observed above the null means people abstract a "prime numbers" rule the model (no primality feature) under-produces, below means the model over-produces it.
results.code:
# name: prime_set_prime_target_contrast
# description: In sets of 2+ examples that are all primes, yes-rate for non-example prime targets minus non-example composite targets of the same parity as the examples' majority; observed above the null means people abstract a "prime numbers" rule the model (no primality feature) under-produces, below means the model over-produces it.
def test_statistic(df):
    primes = set([p for p in range(2, 101) if all(p % q for q in range(2, int(p ** 0.5) + 1))])
    ns = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    sets = ns.unique()
    info = {}
    for s in sets:
        ex = [int(v) for v in s.split(",")]
        allp = len(ex) >= 2 and all(v in primes for v in ex)
        par = int(round(np.mean([v % 2 for v in ex])))
        info[s] = (1 if allp else 0, par, ",".join(str(v) for v in ex))
    isp = ns.map({s: info[s][0] for s in sets}).values.astype(bool)
    par = ns.map({s: info[s][1] for s in sets}).values.astype(int)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    tstr = df["target"].astype(int).astype(str)
    padded = ("," + ns + ",")
    ident = np.array([("," + a + ",") in b for a, b in zip(tstr.values, padded.values)])
    tp = np.isin(t, list(primes))
    base = isp & ~ident & (t > 1)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    a = base & tp
    b = base & ~tp & (t % 2 == par)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: odd_set_parity_contrast
results.description: In sets of 3+ examples that are all odd but share no common factor >=3 and no common final digit, yes-rate for non-example odd targets minus even targets; observed above the null means people abstract an explicit "odd numbers" rule sharper than the model's parity-similarity dimension predicts, below means the model over-weights parity.
results.code:
# name: odd_set_parity_contrast
# description: In sets of 3+ examples that are all odd but share no common factor >=3 and no common final digit, yes-rate for non-example odd targets minus even targets; observed above the null means people abstract an explicit "odd numbers" rule sharper than the model's parity-similarity dimension predicts, below means the model over-weights parity.
def test_statistic(df):
    import math
    from functools import reduce
    ns = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    sets = ns.unique()
    ok = {}
    for s in sets:
        ex = [int(v) for v in s.split(",")]
        ok[s] = (len(ex) >= 3 and all(v % 2 == 1 for v in ex)
                 and reduce(math.gcd, ex) < 3 and len(set(v % 10 for v in ex)) > 1)
    sel = ns.map(ok).values.astype(bool)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    padded = ("," + ns + ",")
    tstr = df["target"].astype(int).astype(str)
    ident = np.array([("," + a + ",") in b for a, b in zip(tstr.values, padded.values)])
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    base = sel & ~ident
    a = base & (t % 2 == 1)
    b = base & (t % 2 == 0)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: round_target_bias
results.description: In sets with no example divisible by 5, yes-rate for multiple-of-10 targets minus yes-rate for all other non-example targets; observed above the null means people have a set-independent preference for round numbers that the model (similarity + set-derived rules only) under-produces, below means people avoid round targets more than predicted.
results.code:
# name: round_target_bias
# description: In sets with no example divisible by 5, yes-rate for multiple-of-10 targets minus yes-rate for all other non-example targets; observed above the null means people have a set-independent preference for round numbers that the model (similarity + set-derived rules only) under-produces, below means people avoid round targets more than predicted.
def test_statistic(df):
    ns = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    sets = ns.unique()
    ok = {s: all(int(v) % 5 != 0 for v in s.split(",")) for s in sets}
    sel = ns.map(ok).values.astype(bool)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    padded = ("," + ns + ",")
    tstr = df["target"].astype(int).astype(str)
    ident = np.array([("," + a + ",") in b for a, b in zip(tstr.values, padded.values)])
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    base = sel & ~ident
    a = base & (t % 10 == 0)
    b = base & (t % 10 != 0)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())
